newsitem.title: UK: Royal&Sun in profit, sees cost savings.
newsitem.headline: Royal&Sun in profit, sees cost savings.

text.p: Newly-merged British composite insurer Royal & Sun Alliance (RSA) on Thursday reported a half-year profit that was ahead of market expectations and said it was on target to achieve full integration by 1998.
It confirmed that it expected to see a reduction of 175 million pounds ($274 million) in annual costs by then, and set out a timetable for how the integration process would proceed.
The merger of Royal and Sun in July created Britain's biggest insurer with a 5.4 billion pounds market capitalisation.

Reporting pro-forma interim pre-tax operating profits of 450 million pounds, down from 514 million last year but ahead of most analysts' forecasts, the group blamed the slide in profits on a 94 million pound increase in worldwide weather losses.

Total long-term business, meanwhile, rose by 12 percent. The company added that merger expenses amounted to 16 million pounds and related to legal and advisers' costs. Shares in RSA edged half a penny up to 412p after touching a session high of 420p.
"These figures are significantly better than expectations," said ABN Amro Hoare Govett analyst Nick Bunker. "The U.K. commercial lines account has been much better than I thought."

Executive deputy chairman Roger Taylor said Royal & Sun had made rapid progress in integrating the two groups, commenting: "We shall be in a strong position to fulfil our potential as a leading insurance company in the U.K. and internationally."
Group chief executive Richard Gamble said the merger would result in more widely-spread profit sources, with the group less dependent on any one area of the world or any one product line.
He told Reuters that the general business in Britain would contribute 110 million pounds to the previously announced 175 million annual cost savings the group expects to see by 1998.

"There will obviously be major savings on accommodation. There will be a reduction in marketing costs. IT (information technology) development, of course, will be a big item, where both companies are at the moment developing IT systems."
RSA said in May that it would cut 5,000 jobs worldwide, with the U.K. accounting for around 80 percent of this. The staff cuts are expected to account for about 60 percent of savings.

At the end of July, the group said it would close 94 branch offices with the loss of around 300 jobs. About 1,000 jobs will go at offices in Liverpool, northern England, and Horsham, southwest of London. Further cuts will be countrywide.

The group on Thursday sent letters to all staff informing them of severance terms, and special merger terms which apply to those taking voluntary or forced redundancy between July 19 1996 and June 30 1998, the target date for completion of the merger.
Setting out a merger timetable for reporters, RSA said 530 senior management positions will be culled by 30 percent by the end of 1998, with a 25 percent reduction expected by October 31.
By then, the group also hopes to have established six centres for servicing personal lines to the broker market, which accounts for around one million RSA general insurance policies.

On the direct sales side, it is the group's current intention to move its three telephone-marketed personal lines businesses much closer together over the course of next year. In the longer term, it would be more efficient to have one brand.
The merged company has three direct brands -- The Insurance Service, Royal Insurance Direct and Sun Alliance Connections -- which together have two million household and motor policies.

Overseas, analysts expect RSA to dispose of business worth up to 100 million pounds in all to eliminate overlap. It has already asked potential buyers for its investment in South African Protea Assurance to enter bids by the end of this month.
The cost of restructuring will be equivalent to about one year's savings and details of this are expected at the year-end.

Gamble said that rates were creeping up in the British private motor insurance sector, a highly competitive market often seen as an indicator of wider future trends. But he added the gains were very small -- single-digit percentile increases.
The group said it sustained 12 million pounds in losses arising from bombings in Manchester and London's Docklands area.
